title: To Sell a Story
author: Marcus Luther
summary: Marcus Luther, a high school English teacher with fifteen years in the classroom, opens with Steinbeck's East of Eden and the word timshel, which is widely held to be a mistranslation that Steinbeck kept because the better story mattered more to him than accuracy. He uses that as a lens on Emily Hanford's Sold a Story, Season 2, which moves beyond reading to look at teaching itself and leans into solutions journalism. Luther argues that the series oversimplifies a messy profession, implies that educators do not believe instruction matters, and tells teachers that designing lessons is not their job. He counters that no lesson designed outside his classroom has ever worked without his own years of trial and error, and that scripted curricula strip away the flexibility that even Hanford praises in Zig Engelmann. He also notes that the Science of Reading has already been co-opted as a marketing label by the publishers it criticized. His closing appeal, borrowed from Leah Mermelstein, is to complicate the story rather than simplify it, with four recommended companion reads.
points: Luther draws a parallel between Steinbeck keeping a mistranslated timshel because it made the better story and education journalism choosing the more convincing narrative over the more accurate one.

He rejects the implication that teachers do not believe instruction matters, calling it gaslighting when teachers are told instruction is vital and then have their hands tied by required curricula and scripts.
Hanford's line that designing lessons is not a teacher's job is, in his experience, contradicted by fifteen years in which no outside-designed lesson worked without his own adaptation.
He observes that the Science of Reading has already become a branding label for the same publishing ecosystem the first season condemned, so a new solution invites a new wave of sellers.
He distinguishes sharing a classroom-rooted strategy from advocating one solution at scale, and asks who is accountable for the quality of impact rather than just its size.
quotes: Steinbeck had settled on the interpretation he wanted to build around, no matter its accuracy, and ran with it all the way until the final page of the novel—in doing so, selling a story of his own that has now cemented itself decisively as the narrative around what timshel means.

But who is attending to that impact? At what point does its quality enter into the discussion rather than just celebrating its quantity? At what point does the incentive around selling a story overwhelm the need for nuance and humility?

I can only speak for myself, but this is precisely the type of gaslighting I’ve been experiencing the last half-decade as a teacher, almost always from folks who are a far-cry away from an actual classroom: the one-two punch of being told that “instruction matters” (duh!) and then having your hands tied in a way that makes it harder to do the actual work of instruction.

Across my fifteen years of experience I’ve never encountered a lesson designed by someone outside the classroom that actually, you know, worked in the classroom without me having to use my own “years of trial and error” to make it work.
In doing so, limiting the capacity of teachers to be responsive to the needs of the students in their classrooms.
You have to ignore a world of context to pretend a story is that simple.

The difference, I think, is between sharing a strategy or perspective—particularly one rooted in authentic classroom experience—and positing “a solution” and advocating for its widespread implementation.
I worry very much that Hanford is once again presenting a simple, convincing story that misrepresents or ignores much of the messiness of the actual reality of teaching.
